USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: We should use the ongoing 13th round of talks in Washington to lock in a Phase One deal — deferring the Oct 15 tariff hike in exchange for concrete Chinese concessions (resumed farm purchases, IP/enforcement commitments) rather than escalating or capitulating. The goal is to relieve the mounting self-inflicted economic damage while holding our leverage, not to settle for a cosmetic deal or walk away.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is real but moderate, not existential. The trade war is now visibly biting the real economy: ISM manufacturing fell to 47.8 in September, the lowest since June 2009 and the second straight month of contraction, an outcome directly attributed to the trade conflict; the Fed has cut rates twice with markets pricing a ~65% chance of another October cut; 10-yr yields collapsed from ~2.5% to ~1.6%. Meanwhile China has already made goodwill moves — a first tariff-exemption list (Sept 11), soybean/pork exclusion signals (Sept 13), and resumed US farm purchases — so the US holds leverage. Consumer sentiment recovered from its 89.8 August trough to 95.5, and retail/business groups are pressing for de-escalation, keeping the US out of existential territory and framing this as a self-inflicted wound. That justifies a +0.35 threat score. The disciplined action is to negotiate a partial Phase One deal that defers the Oct 15 tariff increase and buys reciprocal rollback, rather than max escalation that would deepen the manufacturing recession the ISM report flags and hurt the farm belt; going to full concession is unwarranted because China has not yet met structural demands.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Enter the Washington talks seriously and work toward a limited 'phase one' arrangement that suspends the scheduled December 15 List 4B tariff hike and eases Huawei-related restrictions in exchange for increased US farm imports — but hold firm on structural/tech-transfer and state-subsidy issues. Do not escalate now: further retaliation would only deepen pressure on our own exporters and hand Washington a pretext to raise existing lists. Use our food-import and rare-earth leverage as negotiating capital, not as a trigger for another escalation round.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not existential. The tariff regime is extensive and already biting: List 3 at 25% since May 10 and List 4A at 15% since Sept 1 (timeline), Huawei on the Entity List since May 16 with Google/chip suppliers cutting supply (timeline), and China's exports to the US declining (web: Jan-Jul exports down 2.1% in RMB; ~55% fall in US farm imports to China). The yuan broke 7/ USD in August and Treasury declared China a currency manipulator (timeline), forcing the PBOC to defend stability while exporters report thin or negative margins (web/SCMP). Growth is the slowest in three decades with manufacturing contraction this summer (web/NYT), and Beijing has already had to roll stimulus. This supports a threat reading around +0.45 — clearly high and hitting export hubs and FX, but not existential given China's domestic demand base, rare-earth and food-import leverage, and a US side that itself shows recessionary signals (Fed funds cut to 1.83%, 10-yr at ~1.6%, UM sentiment down to 89.8 in August). The action stance is de-escalation-leaning negotiation: Beijing has already signalled goodwill (Sept 13 soy/pork exemption, Sept 11 tariff-exemption list, timeline) and Washington has delisted 400+ Chinese products and Trump has publicly loosened line on Huawei and needs a win before 2020 (web/SCMP). With high-level talks underway at the decision date and both sides showing de-escalation momentum, the disciplined move is to seek a partial deal that pauses December tariffs rather than escalate, which would shift blame onto China as the intransigent party and deepen the economic cost symmetrically.
